lessons.title: PowerShell and Windows Mental Model
lessons.body:
Phase 01

PowerShell & the
Windows Developer
Mental Model
Learn the shell, paths, PATH lookup, environment
variables, working directories, and failure evidence
before frameworks enter the picture.

Book 1 · Windows & terminal foundations
Course baseline: September 17, 2026 · Windows-first · Project-driven · Production-oriented

Contents
1. The shell mental model                  6. Exit codes

2. Working directories                     7. PowerShell vs Bash

3. Navigation                              8. Mini lab

4. PATH lookup                             9. Common failures

5. Environment variables                 10. Knowledge check

Phase 01 | Page 2 of 6

Your terminal is an engineering
instrument
Many learners treat a terminal as a place where tutorials tell them to paste commands. A full-stack
developer needs a better model: the shell is a programmable interface to the operating system. It
has a current working directory, environment variables, executable lookup rules, command parsing
rules, and an exit status.

You type a command           →         PowerShell parses it     →

Windows locates executable           →       Program runs        →      Exit/output returns

Figure 1 - What happens when you press Enter

Step 1 - Observe where you are

Get-Location
Get-ChildItem
Get-ChildItem -Force

Get-Location answers one of the most important debugging questions in this entire course: where is
this command running? Get-ChildItem lists directory contents; -Force also reveals hidden items
such as .git .

MENTAL MODEL

A relative path is interpreted from the current working directory. If the current directory is
wrong, a perfectly valid command can appear broken.

Step 2 - Navigate without fear

Set-Location $HOME
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path "$HOME\Developer" -Force
Set-Location "$HOME\Developer"
Get-Location

PowerShell aliases such as cd and ls are convenient, but the course sometimes shows the full
cmdlet name so you understand what PowerShell is actually doing.

Phase 01 | Page 3 of 6

Paths with spaces

Set-Location "C:\Users\YourName\Desktop\Full Stack Learning"

Quotes are not decoration. They tell the shell that spaces belong to one path argument.

Step 3 - Inspect commands instead of guessing

Get-Command node -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Get-Command git -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Get-Command pnpm -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
$env:Path -split ';'

Get-Command tells you which executable PowerShell will run. This becomes crucial when two Node
installations exist and the wrong one appears first on PATH.

PowerShell receives: node

Search PATH entries from left to right

First matching node.exe wins

That executable starts

Figure 2 - PATH lookup - Version mismatches often come from executable lookup, not from the project.

Environment variables

Environment variables are named values inherited by processes. They are how shells and
applications discover paths, configuration, and later secrets.

Phase 01 | Page 4 of 6

$env:Path
$env:USERPROFILE
$env:APPDATA
$env:LOCALAPPDATA

TEMPORARY VS PERSISTENT

$env:Path += ";C:\something" changes PATH for the current PowerShell process. It does not
automatically rewrite the user's persistent environment settings. This distinction prevents the
classic “it worked until I opened a new terminal” confusion.

Exit codes and evidence

git --version
$LASTEXITCODE

Human-readable output is useful, but programs also communicate success or failure through exit
codes. Later, CI/CD systems rely on exactly this behavior.

PowerShell vs Bash

Intent                               PowerShell                          Bash equivalent

Environment value                    $env:NAME                           $NAME

Set environment value                $env:NAME="x"                       export NAME=x

Delete file tree                     Remove-Item -Recurse                rm -rf

Home                                 $HOME                               $HOME

Mini lab

1. Create $HOME\Developer\full-stack-2026-lab .
2. Move into it.
3. Create notes.txt with New-Item .
4. List normal and hidden files.
5. Print your PATH one entry per line.
6. Use Get-Command for PowerShell itself.

Phase 01 | Page 5 of 6

Common failures

“The term ... is not recognized”
PowerShell could not resolve the command. Check whether the tool is installed, then Get-Command ,
then PATH. Do not reinstall the entire project.

Path not found
Check Get-Location , spelling, quoting, and whether the directory actually exists.

Knowledge check

1. Why can the same command work in one terminal and fail in another?
2. What does PATH control?
3. Why does a working directory matter to project tools?
4. What is the difference between shell output and an exit code?

Phase 01 · Book 1 · Windows & terminal foundations

Phase 01 | Page 6 of 6

lessons.title: Node Runtime and Version Management
lessons.body:
Phase 01

Node.js Runtime &
Version Management
Install and reason about the JavaScript runtime as a
controlled dependency, not a mysterious global
prerequisite.

Book 2 · Node runtime
Course baseline: September 17, 2026 · Windows-first · Project-driven · Production-oriented

Contents
1. Why Node comes first                         6. PowerShell shell setup

2. LTS vs Current                               7. Install Node 24.21.0

3. Why version managers matter                  8. npm mental model

4. Inspect first                                9. Common errors

5. Install fnm                                10. Checkpoint

Phase 01 | Page 2 of 6

Node.js is the runtime beneath our
JavaScript tooling
Next.js, NestJS, pnpm, Prisma tooling, test runners, build systems, and many developer utilities
ultimately run on Node.js. If the runtime is wrong, every layer above it can become confusing.

Windows process

Node.js runtime 24.21.0 LTS

Package manager and CLIs

Next.js / NestJS / tooling

Figure 1 - Why Node comes before frameworks - Framework commands are programs running on a specific Node
runtime, not independent magic.

Why use LTS instead of Current?

As of September 17, 2026, Node 24.21.0 is an LTS release while Node 26 is the Current line. This
course chooses the LTS line because a long multi-phase curriculum benefits from stability and
ecosystem compatibility more than early access to the newest runtime features.

Why use a version manager?

Installing one global Node version seems simpler until project A requires Node 24 and a future
experiment requires Node 26. A version manager turns runtime selection into an explicit action.

Phase 01 | Page 3 of 6

Project requirements          →       fnm        →         Selected Node version   →

node.exe

Figure 2 - Runtime selection instead of global guesswork

Step 1 - Inspect the machine first

node -v
npm -v
Get-Command node -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Get-Command npm -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

If Node already exists, do not immediately uninstall it. First learn where it came from.

Step 2 - Install fnm on Windows

The official fnm documentation supports WinGet on Windows:

winget install Schniz.fnm

After installation, open a new PowerShell and verify:

fnm --version

Step 3 - Configure fnm for PowerShell

fnm works by updating environment variables for the shell. The official project recommends
evaluating fnm env for the current shell. For a PowerShell profile, a common setup is:

if (-not (Test-Path $PROFILE)) { New-Item -ItemType File -Path $PROFILE -Force }
notepad $PROFILE

Add the shell-initialization line appropriate to the installed fnm version, based on fnm env --shell
powershell . Reopen PowerShell and verify fnm --version .

WHY WE DO NOT BLINDLY OVERWRITE THE PROFILE

PowerShell profiles are personal configuration files. Inspect them before editing. A course
should never erase existing developer configuration just to add one tool.

Phase 01 | Page 4 of 6

Step 4 - Install the locked Node runtime

fnm install 24.21.0
fnm use 24.21.0
node -v
npm -v

Expected baseline:

v24.21.0
11.19.0

Step 5 - Make the choice reproducible

Later we can place a runtime version file in the repository. For now, the important skill is being able
to select and verify the runtime explicitly.

What npm is

npm ships with Node and serves two roles: package registry client and project/package command
tool. In this course we will use pnpm as the primary package manager, but npm remains useful for
bootstrapping pnpm into the user profile when needed.

Common errors

fnm   works, but node does not change
The shell environment probably has not loaded fnm's environment changes. Inspect fnm env --shell
powershell , your PowerShell profile, and Get-Command node .

Wrong Node after opening a new terminal
Check whether fnm initialization loads in that new shell and whether another Node path appears
earlier on PATH.

Company machine blocks WinGet
Use an approved installer mechanism from IT or the fnm release binary. The engineering principle
stays the same: install in user-accessible locations and make PATH explicit.

Phase 01 | Page 5 of 6

Checkpoint

□ fnm --version works.
□ fnm use 24.21.0 works.
□ node -v is v24.21.0.
□ npm -v is 11.19.0.
□ Get-Command node points to the runtime selected through fnm.

lessons.title: pnpm Package Management and Permissions
lessons.body:
Phase 01

pnpm, Package
Management &
Windows Permissions
Understand dependency installation, user-profile
tooling, local executables, build-script approvals, and
why permission errors are filesystem evidence.

Book 3 · Package management
Course baseline: September 17, 2026 · Windows-first · Project-driven · Production-oriented

Contents
1. Package-manager mental model                  6. Core pnpm commands

2. Why pnpm 12.4.2                               7. Local executables

3. Inspect existing tools                        8. Build-script approval

4. Non-admin installation                        9. Checkpoint

5. Corepack EPERM

Phase 01 | Page 2 of 6

pnpm is the package manager for
this course
A package manager resolves dependencies, downloads packages, records exact versions, creates
executable shims, and runs project scripts. pnpm adds a content-addressable store and workspace
features that make it a strong fit for the monorepo we will build in Phase 02.

Read package.json

Resolve dependency graph

Read/write lockfile

Use pnpm content-addressable store

Link project node_modules

Expose package executables

Figure 1 - Package installation lifecycle - A package manager is performing dependency graph and filesystem work,
not merely downloading ZIP files.

Why pnpm 12.4.2?

Phase 00 froze the course baseline. pnpm 12.4.2 was released September 15, 2026 and includes
current security and Windows installation fixes. We keep that exact version throughout the generated
course unless an explicit migration is approved.

Phase 01 | Page 3 of 6

Step 1 - See what already exists

pnpm -v
Get-Command pnpm -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
npm config get prefix

Step 2 - Non-admin user-profile installation

On a machine where the user does not have administrator rights, avoid depending on C:\Program
Files\nodejs for package-manager shims.

npm config set prefix "$env:APPDATA\npm"
npm install -g pnpm@12.4.2
$env:Path += ";$env:APPDATA\npm"
pnpm -v

The temporary PATH append makes the current shell see the user-profile npm bin directory. If your
persistent user PATH does not already contain it, add that directory through Windows user
environment settings or an approved PowerShell profile mechanism.

WHY THIS SOLVES EPERM

Global npm packages are written under the current user profile instead of a protected Program
Files directory. The principle is least privilege: use administrator rights only when the operation
actually requires them.

Corepack and the permission trap

On some Windows installations, corepack enable attempts to create or update shims beside Node in
C:\Program Files\nodejs\ . A standard user may receive EPERM: operation not permitted . That does
not mean pnpm is broken; it means the requested filesystem location is protected.

corepack enable       →         tries protected Node directory        →

Windows access check              →    EPERM

Figure 2 - Permission failure path

Phase 01 | Page 4 of 6

pnpm commands you should understand now

Command                        Meaning

pnpm -v                        Verify the package-manager executable selected by PATH.

pnpm install                   Resolve/install dependencies using the lockfile and manifest.

pnpm add package               Add a runtime dependency to the current package.

pnpm add -D package            Add a development-only dependency.

pnpm remove package            Remove a dependency cleanly.

pnpm exec tool                 Run a locally installed project executable.

pnpm run script                Run a script defined in package.json.

Why local executables matter

Later, Prisma is intentionally local. We will run pnpm exec prisma so the project controls the exact
Prisma version. This is a general professional principle: project tools should usually be versioned with
the project.

Build-script approval

Modern pnpm may refuse unapproved dependency build scripts and report ERR_PNPM_IGNORED_BUILDS .
Treat that as a security signal, not an invitation to disable protection globally.

pnpm approve-builds

Approve only packages the project genuinely requires, and understand why their install scripts
execute.

Checkpoint

□ pnpm -v returns 12.4.2.
□ You know where the pnpm command is resolved from.
□ You can explain local vs global package tools.
□ You can explain why pnpm exec improves reproducibility.
□ You understand what an ignored build script warning is protecting.

Phase 01 | Page 5 of 6

Phase 01 · Book 3 · Package management

Phase 01 | Page 6 of 6

lessons.title: Git and Professional Version Control
lessons.body:
Phase 01

Git & Professional
Version Control
Build a correct mental model of working tree, staging,
commits, diffs, identity, repository hygiene, and safe
engineering history.

Book 4 · Version control
Course baseline: September 17, 2026 · Windows-first · Project-driven · Production-oriented

Contents
1. Git mental model                         7. .gitignore

2. Install Git for Windows                  8. Commit design

3. Configure identity                       9. Branches

4. Practice repository                    10. What not to do

5. Stage and commit                       11. Checkpoint

6. Understand diffs

Phase 01 | Page 2 of 5

Git is the memory of the engineering
process
Git is not merely a cloud backup mechanism. It records intentional snapshots of a project's state so
developers can compare, review, branch, integrate, and recover changes.

Working tree - files you edit

Staging area - changes selected for next snapshot

Commit - named project snapshot

Remote - shared repository history

Figure 1 - Git mental model - The staging area lets you decide exactly what belongs in a commit instead of committing
every modified file by accident.

Step 1 - Install Git for Windows

The official Git install page lists Git 2.55.0(5) as the maintained Windows build as of the Phase 01
baseline. WinGet is supported:

winget install --id Git.Git -e --source winget

Open a new PowerShell and verify:

git --version
Get-Command git

Phase 01 | Page 3 of 5

Step 2 - Configure identity

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global --list

Your Git identity becomes metadata on commits. It is not the same thing as logging in to GitHub.

Step 3 - Create a disposable practice repository

Set-Location "$HOME\Developer\full-stack-2026-lab"
git init
git status
"Phase 01 Git practice" | Set-Content README.md
git status

Step 4 - Stage and commit intentionally

git add README.md
git status
git commit -m "docs: add Phase 01 practice readme"
git log --oneline --decorate -5

Professional habit: read git status before and after every important Git action.

Step 5 - Learn the three diffs

git diff
git diff --staged
git show HEAD

Command                         Question it answers

git diff                        What changed in the working tree but is not staged?

git diff --staged               What exactly will the next commit contain?

git show HEAD                   What did the latest commit record?

Phase 01 | Page 4 of 5

.gitignore is part of architecture hygiene

Generated output, dependencies, logs, editor state, and secrets should not pollute version history.
Later we will ignore node_modules , .env , build artifacts, and other generated files.

Commit design

A good commit is a coherent engineering statement. Avoid a week of unrelated changes under
update stuff . Prefer messages such as feat: add health endpoint , fix: validate missing task
title , or docs: document local setup .

Make one coherent change            →      Review diff             →     Stage intentionally   →

Commit with useful message             →       Continue

Figure 2 - Professional commit loop

Branches - concept before workflow

A branch is a movable name pointing at a commit. We will use branches more seriously when
collaboration and CI/CD arrive. For now, understand that branches isolate lines of work without
duplicating the entire project manually.

What not to do

• Do not commit .env secrets.
• Do not delete .git because a command feels confusing.
• Do not run destructive reset/clean commands copied from the internet before understanding
what they remove.
• Do not use GitHub Desktop or an IDE as a substitute for understanding Git state.

Checkpoint

□ git --version works.
□ Name, email, and default branch are configured.
□ You can explain working tree, staging area, commit, and remote.
□ You can create a repository, stage one file, commit, inspect log, and inspect diffs.

Phase 01 · Book 4 · Version control

lessons.title: VSCode and Developer Workspace
lessons.body:
Phase 01

VS Code & the
Professional Developer
Workspace
Use the editor as a transparent view of the repository,
keep extensions intentional, and understand future
quality gates.

Book 5 · Editor & workspace
Course baseline: September 17, 2026 · Windows-first · Project-driven · Production-oriented

Contents
1. Editor philosophy                       6. Formatter vs linter vs types vs tests

2. Install/verify VS Code                  7. Workspace hygiene

3. Open current folder                     8. Line endings

4. Important panels                        9. Checkpoint

5. Extension discipline

Phase 01 | Page 2 of 5

Your editor should reveal the system,
not hide it
A good editor improves navigation, feedback, refactoring, and inspection while keeping the project
understandable outside the editor. The terminal and repository remain authoritative.

VS Code installation

If VS Code is already installed, verify rather than reinstall. If not, use the official installer or WinGet
according to your organization's policy. After installation:

code --version
Get-Command code

If code is not recognized but VS Code opens normally, the shell command may not yet be on PATH.
Reopen the terminal after installation and inspect PATH before reinstalling the editor.

Open the current folder

Set-Location "$HOME\Developer\full-stack-2026-lab"
code .

The dot means “this directory.” This habit matters because the folder you open becomes the editor's
workspace context.

PowerShell working directory             →        code .            →   VS Code workspace root         →

Explorer / Search / Git / Terminal

Figure 1 - One folder, multiple developer views

Phase 01 | Page 3 of 5

The panels that matter

Explorer                                                  Search
File tree. Use it to understand structure, not            Search across the repository. Essential for
to create random folders.                                 tracing usage and avoiding duplicate
abstractions.

Source Control                                            Integrated Terminal
Convenient view of Git changes. Still verify              Useful, but remember that each terminal
with git status and diffs.                                has its own process environment and
working directory.

Extensions: deliberately small set

Do not install dozens of extensions before the project needs them. Start with language/editor support
that provides clear value. JavaScript/TypeScript support is built in. Later phases can add ESLint,
framework-specific helpers, database tooling, and formatting once the corresponding configuration
exists.

Formatting vs linting vs type checking

Concern                  Main question

Formatter                How should code be laid out?

Linter                   Does the code violate style or correctness rules?

Type checker             Are values used consistently with their types?

Tests                    Does observable behavior meet expectations?

These are different quality gates. Later CI will run them separately so failures are diagnosable.

Workspace hygiene

Use one project root. Avoid nesting accidental duplicate repositories such as taskflow/taskflow .
Avoid placing projects inside folders aggressively synchronized by enterprise backup software if it
causes file-locking or node_modules issues. Prefer a simple development path such as:

Phase 01 | Page 4 of 5

$HOME\Developer\taskflow

Line endings

Windows commonly uses CRLF while many developer tools and servers use LF. Git can normalize line
endings. We will add an explicit .gitattributes only when the repository exists in Phase 02 rather
than generating configuration before there is a project to own it.

Checkpoint

□ code . opens the current folder.
□ You can distinguish editor conveniences from project configuration.
□ You understand formatter, linter, type checker, and tests as separate checks.
□ You have chosen a clean developer workspace path.

lessons.body:
Phase 01

PATH, Permissions &
Environment
Troubleshooting
Diagnose command lookup, EPERM, wrong versions,
shell initialization, working-directory mistakes, and
filesystem interference with evidence.

Book 6 · Troubleshooting
Course baseline: September 17, 2026 · Windows-first · Project-driven · Production-oriented

Contents
1. Debugging ladder                                  7. Execution policy

2. EPERM                                             8. Synced folders

3. Command not recognized                            9. Evidence bundle

4. Wrong versions                                  10. Troubleshooting matrix

5. Terminal environment inheritance                11. Professional rule

6. Wrong working directory

Phase 01 | Page 2 of 6

When tooling fails, diagnose the
operating-system layer first
Environment failures are frustrating because they happen before application code exists. They
become manageable when you classify them: command lookup, working directory, permission,
version, shell initialization, or filesystem lock.

1. Read exact error text

2. Confirm current directory

3. Resolve command with Get-Command

4. Print tool version

5. Inspect PATH / environment

6. Inspect permissions and filesystem

7. Change the smallest thing

Figure 1 - Environment debugging ladder - Debug from evidence. Reinstalling everything is not a diagnosis.

Case 1 - EPERM in Program Files

EPERM: operation not permitted, ... C:\Program Files\nodejs\...

Phase 01 | Page 3 of 6

Layer: filesystem permissions. Hypothesis: a standard user is trying to modify a protected
machine-wide directory. Smallest correction: install the user-owned tool under the user profile or
use an approved installation route. Do not make “run everything as Administrator” your default
workflow.

Case 2 - command not recognized

pnpm : The term 'pnpm' is not recognized...

Layer: executable lookup. Run:

Get-Command pnpm -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
$env:Path -split ';'
Test-Path "$env:APPDATA\npm\pnpm.cmd"

If the file exists but PATH does not include its directory, fix lookup rather than reinstalling the
package.

Case 3 - wrong version

node -v
Get-Command node -All

Multiple executables may exist. Identify which path wins and why. Version managers solve selection
only if the shell loads their environment.

Case 4 - command works only in one terminal

Each terminal is a process with inherited environment state. A terminal opened before installation
may not know about new persistent PATH entries. Close and reopen the shell before assuming
installation failed.

Case 5 - wrong working directory

Symptoms include missing scripts, package manifests not found, Prisma config missing, or Git
reporting that the directory is not a repository.

Phase 01 | Page 4 of 6

Get-Location
Get-ChildItem
Test-Path package.json
Test-Path .git

Case 6 - execution policy confusion

PowerShell execution policy can affect scripts. Do not globally weaken security as a reflex. First
determine exactly which script is blocked and whether the tool offers a signed executable or .cmd
shim. Follow organization policy on managed devices.

Case 7 - synced/locked folders

Cloud sync, antivirus, or corporate endpoint software can temporarily lock large dependency trees. If
repeated filesystem errors occur under a synchronized Desktop/Documents directory, a dedicated
user development folder can reduce interference.

The evidence bundle

Before asking for help, capture:

Get-Location
$PSVersionTable.PSVersion
node -v
npm -v
pnpm -v
git --version
Get-Command node
Get-Command pnpm
Get-Command git

This gives another engineer enough context to reason rather than guess.

Troubleshooting matrix

Symptom                            Likely layer                    First check

Term not recognized                PATH / install                  Get-Command

Wrong version                      PATH / version manager          Get-Command -All

EPERM                              filesystem permissions          target path and ownership

No package.json                    working directory               Get-Location

Phase 01 | Page 5 of 6

Works only in old/new shell          process environment            reopen and compare PATH

Intermittent file locks              sync/AV/filesystem             workspace location

Professional rule

Change one variable at a time. If you reinstall Node,
pnpm, Git, VS Code, and reset PATH simultaneously, you
may fix the symptom while learning nothing about the
cause.

Phase 01 · Book 6 · Troubleshooting

Phase 01 | Page 6 of 6

Phase 01

Hands-On Lab,
Exercises & Phase Exit
Prove the environment through observable
commands, Git history, a verification report, four
exercise levels, and a Phase 01 assessment.

2. Lab B - versions                            7. Knowledge assessment

3. Lab C - command resolution                  8. Answer guide

4. Lab D - Git history                         9. Exit checklist

5. Lab E - environment report                10. Next phase

Phase 01 | Page 2 of 6

Phase 01 hands-on lab: prove the
workstation
This lab turns the phase from reading into observable skill. Complete it in an ordinary PowerShell
session. If your organization prevents an installation step, record the constraint and verify everything
that is permitted.

Lab A - Create a clean learning workspace

$DevRoot = "$HOME\Developer"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $DevRoot -Force
Set-Location $DevRoot
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path "full-stack-2026-lab" -Force
Set-Location "full-stack-2026-lab"
Get-Location

Verification
The current path ends with Developer\full-stack-2026-lab .

Lab B - Verify runtime and tooling

fnm use 24.21.0
node -v
npm -v
pnpm -v
git --version
code --version

Record the output in your notes. Do not continue until unexpected versions have an explanation.

Lab C - Verify command resolution

Get-Command node
Get-Command npm
Get-Command pnpm
Get-Command git
Get-Command code

For every command, write one sentence explaining which directory owns the executable or shim.

Phase 01 | Page 3 of 6

Lab D - Create the first Git history

git init
"# Full-Stack Developer 2026 - Environment Lab" | Set-Content README.md
git add README.md
git diff --staged
git commit -m "docs: initialize environment lab"
git status
git log --oneline -3

Lab E - Build an environment report

Create environment-report.txt using PowerShell output redirection:

"Phase 01 Environment Report" | Set-Content environment-report.txt
"Generated: $(Get-Date -Format o)" | Add-Content environment-report.txt
"PowerShell: $($PSVersionTable.PSVersion)" | Add-Content environment-report.txt
"Node: $(node -v)" | Add-Content environment-report.txt
"npm: $(npm -v)" | Add-Content environment-report.txt
"pnpm: $(pnpm -v)" | Add-Content environment-report.txt
"Git: $(git --version)" | Add-Content environment-report.txt
Get-Content environment-report.txt

This is intentionally not an automated installer. It is evidence that the learner understands
verification.

Exercise ladder

Level 1 - Follow
1. Run every verification command and record expected outputs.
2. Open the lab with code . .
3. Create and commit one Markdown file.

Level 2 - Modify
1. Create a second directory whose name contains spaces and navigate into it correctly.
2. Temporarily append a fake directory to the current shell PATH, print PATH, then close the shell
and explain why it disappeared.
3. Use Get-Command -All node and explain the result.

Level 3 - Implement
1. Write a PowerShell script named verify-environment.ps1 that checks the five tool versions and
exits non-zero if the Node or pnpm version is not the locked baseline.
2. Do not copy a complete solution from the book. Use if , command output, and exit .

Phase 01 | Page 4 of 6

Level 4 - Engineer
Design a small onboarding procedure for a new developer on a restricted corporate laptop. Your plan
must avoid unnecessary administrator rights, preserve existing PowerShell configuration, verify PATH
resolution, and produce an evidence report.

Knowledge assessment

1. Why is Node treated as a project/runtime dependency rather than a permanent global
assumption?
2. Why can corepack enable fail for a non-admin user even when Node itself works?
3. What does pnpm exec protect us from?
4. Why should Get-Location be one of the first commands when a project CLI cannot find its files?
5. What is the difference between Git identity and GitHub authentication?
6. Why is git diff --staged valuable before a commit?
7. What does PATH determine?
8. Why can a freshly installed command require a new terminal?

Answer guide

1. Projects need reproducible runtime compatibility; version managers make selection explicit.
2. It may attempt to write shims into a protected machine-wide Node directory.
3. It resolves a tool from project dependencies, preserving the project's exact version.
4. Relative configuration and manifest discovery depends on the working directory.
5. Git identity is commit metadata; GitHub authentication authorizes access to a remote service.
6. It shows exactly what the next snapshot will contain.
7. Which executable directories the shell searches, in order.
8. The old process inherited environment values before installation changed persistent settings.

Phase exit checklist

□ I can explain working directory, PATH, and environment variables.
□ I can switch to Node 24.21.0 LTS with fnm.
□ npm reports 11.19.0.
□ pnpm reports 12.4.2 from an ordinary user shell.
□ Git is installed, configured, and understood at working-tree/staging/commit level.
□ VS Code opens the current workspace from PowerShell.
□ I can diagnose “command not recognized,” EPERM, and wrong-version problems.
□ I completed the environment report and committed the practice repository.

Phase 01 | Page 5 of 6

What comes next

Phase 02 - Monorepo, pnpm Workspaces & Repository Foundation. We will finally create the
real TaskFlow repository. Phase 01 taught us to trust the workstation; Phase 02 will teach us how to
structure a repository that can contain a Next.js frontend and NestJS backend without premature
abstraction.

Verified workstation

Create TaskFlow repository

Define pnpm workspace

Create apps/ boundary

Establish repository quality gates

Figure 2 - Phase 01 to Phase 02 - The environment becomes infrastructure beneath the real project rather than
something we keep modifying every lesson.

Purpose

lessons.body:
Guided Build Lab — Phase 01: Windows Development Environment & Professional Tooling

Purpose
Build and verify a reproducible Windows development environment without relying on hidden machine state.

Deliverable
A verified toolchain report showing shell, Git, Node, Corepack/pnpm, editor, PATH, ports, and diagnostic commands.

Before you touch the code
Open the previous phase checkpoint, run the repository's verification commands, and make sure Git is clean. A guided lab is useful only when you know which change introduced a failure. Write down the current browser/API/database behavior you expect before modifying anything.

Architecture trace
Windows user environment -> PowerShell -> PATH resolution -> Node runtime -> Corepack/pnpm -> Git -> Editor/terminal -> Project process

Read this flow left to right, then right to left. For each arrow, say what data crosses the boundary, which side trusts the other, and what evidence would prove that this boundary works. This habit prevents framework APIs from becoming disconnected memorization.

Step 1 — Open ordinary PowerShell and record pwd, whoami, and PATH-related observations.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 2 — Install or verify Git and VS Code with user-level installation where possible.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 3 — Install the course Node line with a version manager and prove which executable is active.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 4 — Enable Corepack and activate the repository package-manager version.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 5 — Verify git, node, npm/corepack, pnpm, and editor command availability from a fresh terminal.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 6 — Deliberately create a PATH or port conflict in a safe sandbox and diagnose it with Get-Command/Get-NetTCPConnection.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Useful verification commands
Get-Location
Get-Command node
node --version
corepack --version
pnpm --version
git --version

Do not run commands mechanically. Before each command, predict what successful output should prove. If it fails, capture the exact message and identify whether the failure is environment, dependency, compile-time, runtime, network, authorization, or persistence related.

Checkpoint
When the lab works, inspect git diff. Remove accidental debugging output and unrelated edits. Run type checking/tests/build commands relevant to this phase. Commit the checkpoint with a message that describes the capability added, not merely the files changed.

Explain-back
Without looking at the lesson, explain why each layer in the architecture trace exists, what this phase added to TaskFlow, and what would break if the new responsibility were moved to the wrong layer. If you cannot explain the boundary, repeat the trace before moving on.

lessons.title: Debugging Workshop
lessons.summary:
Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.
lessons.body:
Debugging Workshop — Phase 01: Windows Development Environment & Professional Tooling

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
Windows user environment -> PowerShell -> PATH resolution -> Node runtime -> Corepack/pnpm -> Git -> Editor/terminal -> Project process

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — Terminal still using an old executable after installation
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 2 — EPERM caused by writing to protected locations
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 3 — Different shells resolving different PATH values
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 4 — Port already in use by a forgotten development process
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Do not hide the evidence
Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant.

Debugging exit ticket
Pick one failure from this workshop and write a short incident note: symptom, scope, root cause, fix, verification, and prevention. This is the same communication pattern used in professional bug reports and production incident follow-ups.

lessons.body:
Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Windows Development Environment & Professional Tooling

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 01 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Build and verify a reproducible Windows development environment without relying on hidden machine state.

Required artifact
A verified toolchain report showing shell, Git, Node, Corepack/pnpm, editor, PATH, ports, and diagnostic commands.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can prove which executable a command resolves to.
• Can explain user PATH vs system PATH.
• Can identify a process occupying a port.
• Can recreate the toolchain on another machine from notes.

Independent build sequence
1. Open ordinary PowerShell and record pwd, whoami, and PATH-related observations.
2. Install or verify Git and VS Code with user-level installation where possible.
3. Install the course Node line with a version manager and prove which executable is active.
4. Enable Corepack and activate the repository package-manager version.
5. Verify git, node, npm/corepack, pnpm, and editor command availability from a fresh terminal.
6. Deliberately create a PATH or port conflict in a safe sandbox and diagnose it with Get-Command/Get-NetTCPConnection.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

lessons.title: Mastery Capstone Lab

lessons.body:
Mastery Capstone Lab

This is the transfer exercise for Phase 01: Windows Development Environment & Professional Tooling. The detailed lessons are now closed-book reference material. Your task is to prove that the phase outcome can be reproduced from requirements, repository evidence, and debugging—not by copying a finished implementation.

Target artifact
A verified toolchain report showing shell, Git, Node, Corepack/pnpm, editor, PATH, ports, and diagnostic commands.

Acceptance criteria
- Write the behavior and constraints before implementation.
- Identify the owning layer and every boundary crossed.
- Implement the smallest complete vertical slice.
- Verify the happy path from outside the implementation.
- Demonstrate at least one expected failure path.
- Run the phase-relevant quality checks.
- Review the diff for accidental duplication, leaked responsibilities, missing validation/authorization, and hidden environment assumptions.

Evidence packet
Save the command/request used, expected result, actual result, one failure reproduction, the fix, and a short explanation of why the final responsibility belongs where it does. This packet is more valuable than a screenshot of a green page because it demonstrates repeatable engineering reasoning.

Stretch
Change one requirement after the first implementation. Measure which files must change. If a tiny domain change causes unrelated layers to move, use that evidence to discuss coupling before adding another abstraction.

workshop.why: A guided lesson proves you can follow. A capstone proves you can transfer the model to a requirement with fewer cues.

Deliberately create a PATH or port conflict in a safe sandbox and diagnose it with Get-Command/Get-NetTCPConnection.
